# Ocean crossings: sources and route notes

Research checked September 21, 2026. Story copy is in `history/<period>.md`; the geographic route data is in `tour-oceans.mjs`.

## Reading the map

Three periods show ocean-going networks around 1420, 1500 and 1750 CE. Lanes join ports along the winds and currents that made regular sailing possible; they are not the tracks of named captains, and the dots show direction rather than tonnage. Named voyages (Zheng He, Columbus, da Gama) are used as evidence for the lanes, not drawn as journeys.

## Ming fleets and the monsoon

- [Britannica: Zheng He](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Zheng-He). Seven state expeditions between 1405 and 1433 from Nanjing to Southeast Asia, Ceylon, Calicut, Hormuz, Aden and the East African coast. One two-way lane stands for the whole programme.
- [UNESCO: Melaka and George Town](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1223/). Malacca as the meeting point of Gujarati, Arab, Malay, Javanese and Chinese traders. The Ryukyu lane is drawn fainter because its trade is known mainly from Ryukyuan records.
- The Red Sea–Cairo–Venice spice route and Gujarat's cloth trade to Africa and Southeast Asia are standard accounts of the pre-Portuguese Indian Ocean ([Britannica: Indian Ocean trade](https://www.britannica.com/place/Indian-Ocean)).

## Iberian routes

- [Britannica: Vasco da Gama](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Vasco-da-Gama) and [Britannica: Christopher Columbus](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Christopher-Columbus). The Cape route (Lisbon, Cape Verde, the South Atlantic swing, the Cape, Mozambique, Malindi, Calicut) and the Atlantic circuit (Canaries out, Azores home) follow the winds these voyages established; Cabral's 1500 landfall stands for the Brazil lane.
- [UNESCO: Elmina](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/34/). Gold from the Gold Coast to Lisbon.

## Galleons and companies

- [Britannica: Manila galleon](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Manila-galleon). Acapulco to Manila on the trades, back on the northern westerlies, 1565–1815, exchanging American silver for Chinese silk and porcelain.
- [UNESCO: City of Potosí](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/420/) and [UNESCO: Portobelo–San Lorenzo](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/135/). Silver from Potosí down to Arica and Callao, north to Panama and Portobelo, then in treasure fleets through Cartagena and Havana to Seville and Cádiz; New Spain's silver through Veracruz.
- [Britannica: Dutch East India Company](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Dutch-East-India-Company) and [Britannica: East India Company](https://www.britannica.com/topic/East-India-Company). Cape routes to Batavia, Deshima, Bombay, Madras, Calcutta and Canton; tea, spices, cotton cloth and porcelain to Europe.
- Sugar, tobacco, rice and furs: standard accounts of the Atlantic economy ([Britannica: triangular trade](https://www.britannica.com/topic/triangular-trade), [Britannica: Hudson's Bay Company](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hudsons-Bay-Company)). The African legs of the triangular trade are on the African networks story.

## Deliberate limits

No tonnage, prices or company monopolies are shown. Whaling, the Baltic and Mediterranean trades, Pacific island networks, the Russian fur trade and the overland tea road are omitted. Lanes are schematic; winds and currents are implied by their shape, not modelled.
